verses.translation: And to the messenger{H4397} of the assembly{H5712} of Sardis, write{H3789}: Thus says{H559} the one who has the spirits{H7307} of YHWH{H3068} and the seven{H7651} stars{H3556}: I know{H3045} your deeds{H4639}, for you have a name{H8034} that you are alive{H2416}, yet you are dead{H4191}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses עֵדָה (edah, H5712 — 'assembly/congregation') — the specific Torah word for the congregation of Israel (Num 1:2, 16:2, 27:17, Josh 22:20). Greek has ἐκκλησία (ekklesia — 'church/assembly'). A back-translator from Greek would transliterate as אקלסיה or use קהל (qahal — 'assembly'), NOT the Torah-specific term edah. This word choice ties each assembly directly to Israel's wilderness congregation. Used consistently throughout the chapter.

Uses כֹּה אָמַר (ko amar — 'thus says') — the exact prophetic oracle formula used hundreds of times in the Hebrew prophets: כה אמר יהוה (Isa 43:1, 44:2, 45:1; Jer 2:2; Ezek 2:4, etc.). Greek τάδε λέγει is a simple rendering, but a back-translator from Greek would not necessarily reconstruct this specific prophetic formula. The Hebrew author naturally frames the messages to the assemblies as prophetic oracles.

Hebrew has הָרוּחוֹת יַהְוֶה ('the spirits of YHWH') WITHOUT 'seven' before 'spirits.' Greek has τὰ ἑπτὰ πνεύματα τοῦ θεοῦ ('the seven spirits of God'). Two deviations: (1) Hebrew uses YHWH where Greek uses 'God,' and (2) Hebrew omits 'seven' before 'spirits' while keeping 'seven' only before 'stars.' A back-translator from Greek would include 'seven' before both nouns. The Hebrew 'spirits of YHWH' may echo Isaiah 11:2 where the attributes of the 'Spirit of YHWH' are enumerated.
greek_deviations: Greek: 'the seven spirits of God' (τὰ ἑπτὰ πνεύματα τοῦ θεοῦ). Hebrew: 'the spirits of YHWH' — no number, and YHWH instead of 'God.'
Greek: Σάρδεσιν (Sardesin). Hebrew: זַארְדִּין (Zardin) — a distinct transliteration suggesting independent transmission, not translation from Greek.
translation_notes: 'Assembly' for edah — preserving the Torah congregation connection rather than using 'church.'
'Stars' for kokhavim (H3556) — the standard OT word for stars (Gen 1:16, 15:5, 37:9).
textual_notes: The כה אמר formula appears in all three letters of this chapter (v1, v7, v14), structuring them as prophetic oracles in the pattern of the Hebrew prophets.

verses.translation: Therefore, do not sleep{H3462}, and strengthen{H2388} that which is about to die{H4191}, for I have not found{H4672} your deeds{H4639} whole{H8003} before{H6440} YHWH{H3068}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אַל תִּישַׁן (al tishan — 'do not sleep', from yashen H3462). Greek has γίνου γρηγορῶν ('become watchful'). The Hebrew frames the problem as SLEEPING, not as failure to watch. Sleep carries OT prophetic weight — Jonah sleeping during the storm (Jonah 1:5-6), the disciples sleeping at Gethsemane. A back-translator from Greek 'be watchful' would use שמר (shamar — to guard/watch), not the sleeping verb.

Uses שְׁלֵימָה (shelemah — 'whole/complete', H8003, from the root שלם — shalom). Greek has πεπληρωμένα ('fulfilled/filled'). The Hebrew root שלם means 'whole/complete/at peace' — it's the root of shalom. A back-translator from Greek 'fulfilled' would use מלא (male — 'filled'), not the theologically loaded shalom root. The Hebrew says their deeds lack wholeness/integrity.

Hebrew: לִפְנֵי יַהְוֶה ('before YHWH'). Greek: ἐνώπιον τοῦ θεοῦ μου ('before MY God'). Hebrew uses the divine name YHWH; Greek uses 'my God' with a possessive pronoun. A back-translator from Greek would write לפני אלהי ('before my God'), not use the divine name.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'do not sleep' (negative command). Greek: 'be watchful' (positive command). Opposite framing.
Hebrew: 'whole' (שלמה). Greek: 'fulfilled' (πεπληρωμένα). Different concepts — integrity vs. completion.
Hebrew: 'before YHWH.' Greek: 'before my God.'
translation_notes: 'Whole' for shelemah — capturing the shalom/integrity meaning rather than 'complete' or 'fulfilled.'
שֶׁרוֹצֶה (she-rotzeh) literally means 'that desires/wants,' but in later Hebrew usage means 'is about to.' The biblical root רצה (H7521) means 'to delight in/be pleased with.'

verses.translation: And now, remember{H2142} how you received{H6901} and heard{H8085}, and uphold them, and do teshuvah{H8666}. And if not, I will come{H935} upon you like the thief{H1590}, and you will not know{H3045} at what time I come{H935}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses תְּשׁוּבָה (teshuvah, H8666 — 'returning/repentance,' from root שוב shuv — 'to return'). Greek has μετανόησον (metanoeō — 'change your mind'). Teshuvah is THE Hebrew concept of repentance — a physical turning back to YHWH, a directional reorientation (Jer 3:12,14,22; Hos 14:1-2; Joel 2:12). Greek metanoia is a mental change ('after-thinking'). A back-translator from Greek would use a calque like שנוי דעת ('change of mind') or the late Hebrew חרטה (charatah — regret), NEVER the deeply Jewish teshuvah. This word appears again in v19.

Uses כַּגַּנָּב (ka-gannav — 'like THE thief', H1590) with the definite article. Greek has ὡς κλέπτης ('as a thief') WITHOUT the article. The Hebrew definite article suggests a known/proverbial figure — 'the thief' as an archetype. This grammatical distinction could not arise from back-translating the anarthrous Greek.

Uses זְמַן (zeman — 'time/season') for the unknown moment. Greek has ὥραν (hōra — 'hour'). Hebrew zeman is a broader term for appointed time or season (Eccl 3:1, Neh 2:6, Est 9:27); Greek specifies a precise 'hour.' A back-translator from Greek would use שעה (sha'ah — 'hour'), not the broader zeman.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: תשובה ('returning'). Greek: μετανόησον ('change your mind'). Fundamentally different concepts of repentance.
Hebrew: 'at what time' (זמן — season). Greek: 'what hour' (ὥραν — specific hour).
Hebrew: 'like THE thief' (definite). Greek: 'as a thief' (indefinite).
translation_notes: 'Teshuvah' left untranslated — no English word captures the Hebrew concept of physical, directional return to YHWH.
מְקַיֵּים (meqayem — 'upholding/fulfilling') from a later Hebrew form related to root קום (qum, H6965 — to rise/establish). No standard Strong's number for this piel form.
textual_notes: The thief imagery connects to Joel 2:9 — 'they enter through the windows like a thief' (כַּגַּנָּב) — using the same definite article construction. This is an OT prophetic motif.

verses.translation: And also your name{H8034} is heard{H8085} in Sardis — those who did not defile their garments{H899}, and they shall walk{H1980} with me in white{H3836} garments{H899}, for they are worthy of this.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Hebrew has שִׁמְךָ נִשְׁמָע ('your name is heard,' שם/שמע). Greek has ὀλίγα ὀνόματα ('a few names,' meaning a few people). These are entirely different statements! Hebrew says 'your name/reputation is known'; Greek says 'you have few names/people.' The Hebrew contains an assonance — שִׁמְךָ (shimkha, 'your name') and נִשְׁמָע (nishma, 'is heard') echo each other phonetically (shin-mem/shin-mem-ayin). This Hebrew wordplay is invisible in Greek and could not arise from back-translation.

Uses תֵּלְכוּ (telkhu — 'shall walk', from halakh H1980). Greek has περιπατήσουσιν (peripatesousin — 'shall walk around'). Both mean 'walk,' but the Hebrew verb הלך is THE verb of following YHWH's ways in the OT — 'walking in his statutes' (Lev 26:3), 'walking before YHWH' (Gen 17:1). The 'walking with me' (עמי) echoes Enoch who 'walked with God' (Gen 5:22,24).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'your name is heard' (positive reputation statement). Greek: 'you have a few names' (numerical statement about people). Entirely different meaning.
Hebrew: 'for they are worthy of this' (לזה). Greek: 'for they are worthy' — omits 'of this.'
translation_notes: טִנְּפוּ (tinfu — 'defiled/soiled') is a later Hebrew verb with no standard Strong's number. The biblical equivalent would be טמא (tame — H2930, 'to make unclean').
רְאוּיִם (re'uyim — 'worthy/fitting') is a later Hebrew adjective, no standard Strong's.

verses.translation: And whoever overcomes{H5329} shall walk{H1980} in white{H3836} garments{H899}, and I will not blot out{H4229} his name{H8034} from the scroll{H5612} of life{H2416}, and I will make known{H3045} his name{H8034} before{H6440} my Father{H1} and before{H6440} his messengers{H4397}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מוֹדִיעַ (modia — 'make known', hifil of yada H3045). Greek has ὁμολογήσω (homologēsō — 'I will confess/acknowledge'). These are fundamentally different acts: 'making known' (revealing to those who don't yet know) vs. 'confessing/acknowledging' (declaring before those who already know). A back-translator from Greek ὁμολογέω would use הודה (hodah — 'to confess/give thanks'), NOT the causative of ידע (yada).

Uses אֶמְחֶה (emcheh — 'I will blot out', from machah H4229) — the EXACT verb from Exodus 32:32-33 where YHWH says 'Whoever has sinned against me, I will blot him out (אֶמְחֶנּוּ) of my book.' The Hebrew author uses Moses's precise vocabulary. Greek ἐξαλείψω is equivalent but a back-translator would not necessarily reach for this specific Exodus verb.

Uses תֵּלֵךְ (telekh — 'shall walk', from halakh H1980) for wearing white garments. Greek has περιβαλεῖται (peribaleitai — 'shall be clothed/wrapped'). Hebrew says the overcomer will WALK in white; Greek says the overcomer will be CLOTHED in white. Different verbs entirely — walking implies active movement; being clothed implies passive reception.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'make known' (מודיע, revealing). Greek: 'confess/acknowledge' (ὁμολογήσω, declaring).
Hebrew: 'shall walk in white garments.' Greek: 'shall be clothed in white garments.' Different verbs.
Hebrew: מִסֵּפֶר ('from the scroll' — sefer, a scroll). Greek: ἐκ τῆς βίβλου ('from the book' — biblos). Hebrew specifies a scroll; Greek specifies a codex/book.
translation_notes: 'Scroll' for sefer (H5612) — preserving the ancient format. A sefer in the biblical period was always a scroll, not a bound book.
'Make known' for modia — the causative of 'to know,' implying revelation of something previously hidden.
textual_notes: Exodus 32:32-33 — 'And YHWH said to Moses: Whoever has sinned against me, him will I blot out (אמחנו) from my book (ספרי).' The vocabulary sefer + machah in the same context is an Exodus echo.

verses.translation: Whoever has ears{H241} hears{H8085} what the spirit{H7307} says{H559} to the assembly{H5712}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses SINGULAR הָעֵדָה ('the assembly'). Greek has PLURAL ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις ('the assemblies/churches'). A back-translator from Greek plural would write העדות (ha-edot — plural). The Hebrew singular addresses each assembly individually as 'the assembly,' reflecting the Torah concept of Israel as one edah.

Hebrew: שׁוֹמֵעַ ('hears' — present participle, stating a fact). Greek: ἀκουσάτω ('let him hear' — imperative, issuing a command). The Hebrew states that the one with ears DOES hear; the Greek commands him TO hear. Different moods entirely.
Uses אָזְנַיִם (oznayim — 'ears', DUAL form, both ears). Greek has οὖς (ous — 'ear', SINGULAR). The Hebrew dual emphasizes hearing with BOTH ears — full attentiveness.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: singular 'assembly.' Greek: plural 'assemblies.'
Hebrew: 'hears' (indicative). Greek: 'let him hear' (imperative).
Hebrew: 'ears' (dual — both ears). Greek: 'ear' (singular).
textual_notes: This refrain appears in all seven letters (Rev 2-3). The formula echoes Deuteronomy 29:4 and Isaiah 6:9-10 — the theme of ears that hear and ears that don't.

verses.translation: And to the messenger{H4397} of the assembly{H5712} of Philadelphia, write{H3789}: Thus says{H559} the Holy One{H6918} and the Faithful One{H539}, the one who has the key{H4668} of David{H1732} — the opener{H6605}, and no one is able{H3201} to shut{H5462}; the shutter{H5462}, and no one is able{H3201} to open{H6605}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL WORDPLAY: The Hebrew creates a triple wordplay on the root פתח (patach — 'to open'): מַפְתֵּחַ (mafteach — 'key,' literally 'that which opens'), הַפּוֹתֵחַ (ha-poteach — 'the opener'), and the infinitive לִפְתּוֹחַ (liftoach — 'to open'). In Hebrew, the word 'key' SHARES ITS ROOT with 'open' — the key IS 'the opener.' This wordplay is IMPOSSIBLE in Greek, where κλείς ('key') and ἀνοίγω ('open') share no root. A back-translator could never reconstruct this triple פתח wordplay. This wordplay continues in v8 and v20.

Uses הַנֶּאֱמָן (ha-ne'eman — 'the Faithful One,' from root אמן aman, H539). Greek has ὁ ἀληθινός (ho alēthinos — 'the True One'). Different attributes: faithfulness/trustworthiness vs. truth/genuineness. A back-translator from 'the True One' would use הָאֲמִתִּי (ha-amiti — 'the truthful one') or הַיָּשָׁר (ha-yashar — 'the upright one'), not ne'eman. Note: ne'eman shares root אמן with אָמֵן (Amen) in v14 — a cross-verse wordplay.

Uses הַמַּפְתֵּחַ שֶׁל דָּוִד ('the key of David,' H4668) — a DIRECT quote from Isaiah 22:22: וְנָתַתִּי מַפְתֵּחַ בֵּית דָּוִד עַל שִׁכְמוֹ ('and I will place the key of the house of David upon his shoulder'). The Hebrew uses the identical word מפתח from Isaiah. Greek has τὴν κλεῖν Δαυΐδ ('the key of David'). A back-translator could use מפתח, but the triple פתח wordplay (key-opener-open) reveals an author thinking in Hebrew roots, not translating from Greek.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the Faithful One' (נאמן). Greek: 'the True One' (ἀληθινός). Different attributes.
Hebrew adds יוּכַל ('is able') — 'no one IS ABLE to shut/open.' Greek has simply οὐδεὶς κλείσει/ἀνοίγει ('no one shall/does shut/open'). Hebrew emphasizes INABILITY.
translation_notes: 'Key' for mafteach (H4668) — this word appears in Isaiah 22:22, Judges 3:25, and 1 Chronicles 9:27. It literally means 'opener' (the tool that opens).
'Opener' and 'shutter' preserve the participial forms that highlight the authority of the key-holder.
textual_notes: Isaiah 22:22 — 'And I will place the key (מפתח) of the house of David upon his shoulder; and he shall open (ופתח), and none shall shut (ואין סגר); and he shall shut (וסגר), and none shall open (ואין פתח).' The Hebrew Revelation reproduces Isaiah's vocabulary with the same roots פתח and סגר.

verses.translation: I know{H3045} your deeds{H4639}. See{H7200}! I have set{H5414} before{H6440} you an open{H6605} opening{H6607}, and no one is able{H3201} to shut{H5462} it, for you have a little{H4592} strength{H3581}, and you have guarded{H8104} my word{H1697} and have not denied my name{H8034}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL WORDPLAY: פֶּתַח פָּתוּחַ (petach patuach — 'an open opening'). BOTH words are from the SAME root פתח! This is a Hebrew figura etymologica (cognate accusative) that intensifies meaning — the opening is emphatically, inherently open. Greek has θύραν ἀνεῳγμένην ('an opened door') — where 'door' (θύρα) and 'opened' (ἀνοίγω) share NO root. A back-translator from Greek would write דלת פתוחה ('an opened door'), not the wordplay petach patuach. This continues the פתח wordplay chain from v7.

Uses כּוֹפֵר (kofer — 'denying') from the root כפר. In biblical Hebrew, this root means 'to cover/atone' (H3722) — it is the root of כִּפֻּר (kippur, as in Yom Kippur) and כֹּפֶר (kofer — 'ransom/atonement price,' H3724). In later Hebrew, כפר ב came to mean 'to deny/disbelieve in.' The same root thus connects denial and atonement — denying the name is the opposite of receiving atonement. This semantic range is unique to Hebrew. Greek ἠρνήσω ('denied') has no such atonement connection.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: פֶּתַח ('opening,' from root פתח). Greek: θύραν ('door'). Hebrew uses 'opening'; Greek uses 'door.' Different nouns.
Hebrew: כופר ('denying,' root כפר). Greek: ἠρνήσω ('denied,' root ἀρνέομαι). The Hebrew root carries atonement overtones absent from the Greek.
translation_notes: 'Opening' for petach (H6607) rather than 'door' — preserving the root connection with mafteach (key) and poteach (opener) from v7.
'Guarded' for shamarta (H8104) — shamar means to watch over, protect, and keep, as in 'to guard the garden' (Gen 2:15) and 'to guard the commandments' (Deut 5:29).
כּוֹפֵר (kofer) in the 'deny' sense has no standard Strong's number; this usage is post-biblical.

verses.translation: See{H7200}! I will give{H5414} to those who are from the fellowship{H2266} of the Adversary{H7854}, who say{H559} they are Yehudim{H3064} but are not — only deceivers. See{H7200}! I will cause them to come{H935} and bow in prayer{H6419} at your feet{H7272} and to acknowledge{H5234} that I have loved{H157} you.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses חַבְרוּתַת (chavrutat — 'fellowship/companionship of'), from root חבר (chaver, H2266/H2270 — 'companion/friend'). Greek has συναγωγῆς (sunagōgēs — 'synagogue/gathering'). The Hebrew חברותא (chavruta) is a uniquely Hebraic/Aramaic term for intimate fellowship or study partnership — a concept central to rabbinic culture. A back-translator from Greek 'synagogue' would write בֵּית כְּנֶסֶת (beit knesset — 'house of gathering') or transliterate סינאגוגא, NEVER use the distinctly Jewish relational term chavruta. The choice implies an intimate circle of the Adversary, not merely a 'synagogue.'

Uses הַשָּׂטָן (ha-satan — 'the Adversary,' H7854) WITH the definite article, preserving it as a common noun with article ('the accuser/adversary'), as in Job 1:6-7, 2:1 and Zechariah 3:1-2. Greek has Σατανᾶ (Satana) as a PROPER NAME without article. The Hebrew treats this as a title — 'the adversary' — maintaining OT usage. A back-translator from Greek's proper name would omit the article.

Uses לִתְפַּלֵּל (lehitpalel — 'to pray/bow in prayer,' H6419, hitpael of פלל). This is THE Hebrew word for Jewish prayer — the reflexive of palal ('to judge'), implying self-examination before God. Greek has προσκυνήσωσιν (proskunēsōsin — 'to worship/bow down'). A back-translator from Greek would use לְהִשְׁתַּחֲווֹת (lehishtachavot — 'to prostrate/bow down'), NOT the prayer-specific lehitpalel. The Hebrew implies they will come and PRAY at the feet of the faithful — a far deeper act than mere bowing.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: חברותת ('fellowship/companionship'). Greek: συναγωγή ('synagogue/gathering'). Different social concepts.
Hebrew: לתפלל ('to pray/bow in prayer'). Greek: προσκυνήσωσιν ('to worship/bow down'). Different acts.
Hebrew: כוזבים ('deceivers/liars,' from כזב). Greek: ψεύδονται ('they lie'). Hebrew uses a noun (they ARE liars); Greek uses a verb (they lie).
translation_notes: 'Fellowship' for chavrutat — capturing the intimate relational concept rather than the institutional 'synagogue.'
'Adversary' for ha-satan — preserving the common noun with article, as in the OT, rather than treating it as a proper name.
'Bow in prayer' for lehitpalel — the hitpael of palal carries both prayer and physical bowing.
וּלְהַכִּיר (ulehakir — 'and to acknowledge,' hifil of nakar H5234) means 'to recognize/identify' — more relational than Greek γνῶσιν ('they will know').
textual_notes: Isaiah 60:14 — 'The sons of those who oppressed you shall come bending low to you, and all who despised you shall bow down (והשתחוו) at the soles of your feet.' The Hebrew Revelation may allude to this Isaiah prophecy but uses the prayer verb instead of the bowing verb.

verses.translation: Because you have guarded{H8104} the utterance of my hope{H8615}, so I will guard{H8104} you from the time{H6256} of trial that comes{H935} upon the earth{H776}, to test those who dwell upon the earth{H776}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses תִּקְוָתִי (tiqvati — 'my hope,' from tikvah H8615). Greek has ὑπομονῆς μου (hupomonēs mou — 'my patience/endurance'). These are ENTIRELY different concepts: hope (expectation/waiting for something good) vs. patience (enduring hardship). A back-translator from Greek 'patience' would use סַבְלָנוּת (savlanut — 'patience'), אֹרֶךְ אַפַּיִם (erekh apayim — 'long-suffering'), or סֵבֶל (sevel — 'endurance'), NEVER the hope-word tikvah. Furthermore, tikvah in Hebrew ALSO means 'cord/thread' (Josh 2:18, 21 — Rahab's scarlet cord of tikvah). The 'utterance of my cord/hope' carries a dual meaning impossible in Greek.

Uses הַדִּיבּוּר (ha-dibbur — 'the utterance/speech') — from root דבר (davar, H1696). This is the specific word for divine speech, as in the עֲשֶׂרֶת הַדִּבְּרוֹת (Aseret ha-Dibbrot — 'the Ten Utterances/Commandments'). Greek has τὸν λόγον (ton logon — 'the word'). A back-translator from Greek would use דָּבָר (davar — 'word'), not the elevated dibbur. The Hebrew implies guarding a divine utterance, not merely a word.

Uses שָׁמַרְתָּ ... אֶשְׁמוֹר (shamarta ... eshmor — 'you guarded ... I will guard') — the SAME root שמר (shamar, H8104) for both human and divine action, creating a reciprocal bond: 'you guarded my utterance, therefore I guard you.' Greek uses the same root τηρέω (tēreō) for both, but the Hebrew שמר carries the weight of Genesis 2:15 (guarding the garden) and Psalm 121 (YHWH who guards Israel). The Hebrew reciprocity is structural.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: תקותי ('my hope'). Greek: ὑπομονῆς μου ('my patience/endurance'). Fundamentally different concepts.
Hebrew: דיבור ('utterance'). Greek: λόγον ('word'). Different registers of speech.
Hebrew: הָעֵת ('the time/season'). Greek: τῆς ὥρας ('the hour'). Hebrew = broader season; Greek = specific hour.
Greek adds τῆς οἰκουμένης ὅλης ('the whole inhabited world') — Hebrew has simply הָאָרֶץ ('the earth').
translation_notes: 'Utterance' for dibbur — preserving the elevated register of divine speech, distinct from the common 'word' (davar).
'Hope' for tikvah — left as the primary meaning, though the 'cord/thread' secondary meaning enriches the image.
textual_notes: The tikvah/cord connection to Joshua 2:18 is striking: Rahab was saved from destruction by the tikvah (scarlet cord); here the assembly is saved from trial by guarding the 'utterance of my tikvah.' Both involve being protected during judgment.

verses.translation: See{H7200}! I come{H935} speedily. Guard{H8104} what you have, so that no one takes{H3947} your crown{H3804}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כֶּתֶר (keter, H3804 — 'crown') — the ROYAL crown word from Esther (Est 1:11, 2:17, 6:8). Greek has στέφανον (stephanon — 'wreath/victory crown'). These are fundamentally different types of crowns: keter is a royal diadem of sovereignty (Persian/royal usage); stephanos is a wreath awarded for athletic or military victory. A back-translator from Greek στέφανος would use עֲטָרָה (atarah — 'wreath/garland,' H5850) or transliterate, NOT reach for the royal keter. The Hebrew author gives the overcomer a ROYAL crown, not merely a victor's wreath.

Uses שְׁמוֹר (shemor — 'guard,' from shamar H8104). Greek has κράτει (kratei — 'hold fast/seize'). The Hebrew verb means to watch over and protect (as a sentinel); the Greek verb means to grip or hold onto. A back-translator from Greek would use אחז (achaz — 'to grasp') or החזק (hecheziq — 'to hold fast'), not the guardian-verb shamar.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: כתר ('royal crown'). Greek: στέφανος ('victor's wreath'). Different types of crown.
Hebrew: שמור ('guard/protect'). Greek: κράτει ('hold fast/grip'). Different verbs.
translation_notes: 'Crown' for keter — the royal diadem, not a wreath. This is the crown of Esther and the Persian kings.
בִּמְהֵרָה (bimherah — 'speedily') is a Hebrew liturgical word familiar from Jewish prayer ('bimhera v'yameinu — speedily and in our days'). No standard Strong's number.

verses.translation: Whoever overcomes{H5329} — I will write{H3789} upon him the name{H8034} of my Elohim{H430}, and the name{H8034} of the new{H2319} Yerushalayim{H3389}, the city{H5892} of my Elohim{H430} that comes{H935} from the heavens{H8064} to the earth{H776} from my Elohim{H430}, and also my new{H2319} name{H8034}.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew OMITS the entire clause about being made a pillar in the temple: Greek has ποιήσω αὐτὸν στῦλον ἐν τῷ ναῷ τοῦ θεοῦ μου, καὶ ἔξω οὐ μὴ ἐξέλθῃ ἔτι ('I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go out no more'). This substantial clause is ABSENT from Hebrew. If the Hebrew were a back-translation from Greek, omitting such a vivid and theologically significant image would be inexplicable. Its absence suggests the Greek translator added this pillar imagery — possibly influenced by the actual pillars of the Jerusalem temple (Jachin and Boaz, 1 Kings 7:21).
greek_deviations: Greek adds the entire 'pillar in the temple' clause — absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: מֵאֱלֹהַי ('of/from my Elohim') appears three times. Greek also has τοῦ θεοῦ μου ('of my God') three times. Parallel structure preserved, but Hebrew uses the distinctly Hebraic 'Elohim.'
translation_notes: הֶחָדָשׁ (he-chadash — 'the new,' masculine) modifying ירושלים. Jerusalem in Hebrew can take either masculine or feminine agreement.
textual_notes: The three-fold repetition of 'my Elohim' (אלהי) emphasizes the personal covenant relationship. Isaiah 62:2 prophesies: 'You shall be called by a new name (שם חדש) which the mouth of YHWH will designate' — the 'new name' concept has OT roots.

verses.translation: Whoever has ears{H241} hears{H8085} what the spirit{H7307} says{H559} to the assembly{H5712}.

greek_deviations: Same deviations as v6: Hebrew singular 'assembly' vs. Greek plural 'assemblies'; Hebrew indicative 'hears' vs. Greek imperative 'let him hear'; Hebrew dual 'ears' vs. Greek singular 'ear.'

verses.translation: And to the messenger{H4397} of the assembly{H5712} of Laodicea, write{H3789}: Thus says{H559} Amen{H543}, the faithful{H539} witness{H5707}, the beginning{H8462} of the creations.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL WORDPLAY: אָמֵן (Amen, H543) followed immediately by נֶאֱמָן (ne'eman — 'faithful,' H539). BOTH words derive from the SAME Hebrew root אמן (aman — 'to be firm/established/faithful'). Amen IS 'the faithful one' — the name and the attribute share one root. In Greek, Ἀμήν is a transliterated Hebrew word, and πιστός ('faithful') comes from πείθω ('to persuade'). The root connection is INVISIBLE in Greek. This also connects back to הַנֶּאֱמָן (the Faithful One) in v7 — the same root spans both letters.

Uses PLURAL בְּרִיאוֹת (beriot — 'creations/creatures'). Greek has SINGULAR κτίσεως (ktiseōs — 'creation'). The Hebrew plural implies multiple acts of creation or multiple created orders. A back-translator from Greek singular would use בְּרִיאָה (beriah — singular 'creation'), not the plural.

Hebrew: הָעֵד נֶאֱמָן ('the faithful witness' — two words). Greek: ὁ μάρτυς ὁ πιστὸς καὶ ἀληθινός ('the faithful AND TRUE witness' — adds 'and true'). The Hebrew is more concise; the Greek adds ἀληθινός ('true'). Hebrew omits 'true' because ne'eman already encompasses both faithfulness and truthfulness in the Hebrew semantic range.
greek_deviations: Greek adds καὶ ἀληθινός ('and true') — absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: plural 'creations' (בריאות). Greek: singular 'creation' (κτίσεως).
Greek adds τοῦ θεοῦ ('of God') after 'creation' — absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Amen' left untranslated — it is a Hebrew word meaning 'firm/certain/so be it,' functioning here as a divine title: 'The Certain One.'
הַתְּחִלָּה (ha-techillah, H8462 — 'the beginning') appears in Gen 13:3, 41:21, 43:18-20; Ruth 1:22; Neh 11:17.
בְּרִיאוֹת (beriot) is from root ברא (bara, H1254 — 'to create'). The noun form is post-biblical.
textual_notes: Isaiah 65:16 — 'Whoever blesses himself in the earth shall bless himself in the God of Amen (אלהי אמן).' Amen as a divine title/attribute has OT precedent.

verses.translation: I know{H3045} your deeds{H4639}, that you are not cold{H7119} and not hot{H2525}. Perhaps{H194} you would be cold{H7119} or hot{H2525}!

one_way_hebrew: Uses אוּלַי (ulai — 'perhaps/maybe,' H194). Greek has ὄφελον (ophelon — 'I wish/would that'). These express DIFFERENT attitudes: Hebrew אולי is a tentative suggestion, a gentle 'perhaps' (Gen 18:24, 24:5, Num 22:11); Greek ὄφελον is a strong wish bordering on lament. A back-translator from Greek's strong wish would use מי יתן (mi yitten — 'who would give that...,' the standard Hebrew optative), NOT the mild, exploratory ulai.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: אולי ('perhaps'). Greek: ὄφελον ('I wish'). Different intensity — gentle suggestion vs. strong desire.
translation_notes: קַר (qar, H7119 — 'cold') appears in Prov 25:25, Gen 8:22. חָם (cham, H2525 — 'hot/warm') appears in Gen 8:22, Josh 9:12.

verses.translation: But since you are not cold{H7119} and not hot{H2525}, on account of this I spit{H3417} you out from my mouth{H6310}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses יֹרֵק (yoreq — 'spit,' from yaraq H3417). Greek has μέλλω ἐμέσαι (mellō emesai — 'I am about to VOMIT'). These are completely different bodily acts: spitting is an act of REJECTION and SHAMING in Hebrew culture (Num 12:14 — 'If her father had spat in her face'; Deut 25:9 — spitting in the face of one who refuses levirate duty; Isa 50:6 — 'I did not hide my face from shame and spitting'). Vomiting is an involuntary physiological response. A back-translator from Greek 'vomit' would use הֵקִיא (heqi — 'to vomit,' from root קיא H7006, Lev 18:28, Prov 23:8, Jonah 2:10), NOT the shaming act of spitting. The Hebrew author invokes the Torah's act of public rejection.

Hebrew: present tense יֹרֵק ('I spit' — ongoing/present). Greek: future/imminent μέλλω ἐμέσαι ('I am ABOUT TO vomit'). Hebrew presents the rejection as already underway; Greek presents it as impending. Different temporal framing.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'spit' (ירק — act of shaming). Greek: 'vomit' (ἐμέω — physiological response). Entirely different imagery.
Hebrew: present tense ('I spit'). Greek: imminent future ('I am about to vomit').
Hebrew lacks any equivalent of χλιαρός ('lukewarm') — Greek inserts this term; Hebrew simply restates 'not cold and not hot.'
translation_notes: 'Spit' for yoreq — preserving the Hebrew act of public rejection/shaming, distinct from vomiting.
The consonantal text ירק could theoretically be read as 'green/vegetable' (yerek), but contextual meaning is clearly 'to spit' (yaraq, as in Lev 15:8).
textual_notes: Numbers 12:14 — 'If her father had surely spit (ירק ירק) in her face, would she not be ashamed seven days?' Leviticus 15:8 — 'If the one with a discharge spits (ירק) on one who is clean.' The spitting verb carries Torah-level significance as an act of rejection.

verses.translation: And you say{H559}: 'I am wealthy{H6239} and I have enough{H1767}, and I have no need of anything{H1697}.' But you do not know{H3045} that you are poor{H6041} and destitute{H34}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses the word pair עָנִי וְאֶבְיוֹן (ani v'evyon — 'poor and destitute,' H6041 + H34) — only TWO descriptors. Greek has FIVE: ταλαίπωρος καὶ ἐλεεινὸς καὶ πτωχὸς καὶ τυφλὸς καὶ γυμνός ('wretched and pitiable and poor and blind and naked'). The Hebrew עני ואביון is a FIXED OT word pair appearing as a unit in Deut 15:11, 24:14; Ps 35:10, 37:14, 40:17, 70:5, 72:13, 86:1, 109:16,22; Jer 22:16; Ezek 16:49; Amos 8:4. A back-translator from Greek's five-word list would NEVER independently reconstruct this specific two-word OT pairing. The Hebrew is a concise prophetic formula; the Greek is an expanded rhetorical list.

Uses דַּי (dai, H1767 — 'enough/sufficient') — a distinctly Hebrew word. Greek has πεπλούτηκα ('I have become rich'). Hebrew says 'I have enough'; Greek says 'I have become wealthy.' Different claims: sufficiency vs. enrichment.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 2 descriptors — 'poor and destitute' (עני ואביון). Greek: 5 descriptors — 'wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, naked.' Hebrew omits 'blind and naked.'
Hebrew: 'I have enough' (dai). Greek: 'I have become rich' (πεπλούτηκα). Different self-assessments.
Hebrew: 'I have no need of anything' (אינה צורך לשום דבר). Greek: 'I have need of nothing' (οὐδενὸς χρείαν ἔχω). Similar but Hebrew uses later idiom.
translation_notes: 'Destitute' for evyon (H34) — this word specifically denotes one who is needy/lacking/in want. Together with ani ('poor'), it forms the classic OT pair for the oppressed class whom Torah commands Israel to protect.
צוֹרֶךְ (tzorekh — 'need') is a later Hebrew noun with no standard Strong's number.
textual_notes: Hosea 12:8 (Hebrew 12:9) — 'And Ephraim said: Surely I have become rich (עשרתי), I have found wealth for myself.' The self-deceived boast of wealth has prophetic precedent. The Laodicean boast echoes Ephraim's.

verses.translation: And I give my counsel{H6098} to you: buy{H7069} gold{H2091} from me, and clothe{H3847} yourself in white{H3836} garments{H4403}, and anoint{H4886} your eyes{H5869} with oil{H8081} so that you may see{H7200}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בַּשֶּׁמֶן (ba-shemen — 'with oil,' H8081). Greek has κολλούριον (kollourion — 'eye-salve'). Shemen is the standard OT anointing oil (Ex 30:25, 1 Sam 16:13). A back-translator from Greek κολλούριον (a specific Greco-Roman medicinal product for eyes) would transliterate the Greek term or describe an eye-salve, NEVER use שמן (shemen — generic oil). The Hebrew author prescribes the biblical anointing substance; the Greek translator converted it to a culturally familiar Greco-Roman remedy. Laodicea was famous for its eye-salve industry — the Greek may reflect local knowledge that the Hebrew original did not possess.

CRITICAL: Uses מָשַׁחְתָּ (mashachta — 'and you shall anoint,' from mashach H4886) — the ROOT of מָשִׁיחַ (Mashiach — 'Messiah/Anointed One'). This is the specific verb for priestly and royal anointing (Ex 30:26, 1 Sam 16:13, 1 Kings 1:39). Greek ἐγχρῖσαι (enchrisai) is from χρίω (chriō) — the root of Χριστός (Christos). BOTH words are 'anoint' roots, but the Hebrew mashach carries the full weight of Torah anointing — kings, priests, and the tabernacle were all 'mashach'd.' The Hebrew reader hears Messianic overtones in 'anoint your eyes.'

Uses עֲצָתִי (atzati — 'my counsel,' from etsah H6098). This is the OT word for divine/wise counsel (Isa 9:6 — 'Wonderful Counselor'; Ps 33:11 — 'the counsel of YHWH stands forever'; Prov 19:21 — 'the counsel of YHWH, it will stand'). Greek: συμβουλεύω ('I advise'). A back-translator would use a verb form; the Hebrew uses the noun 'my counsel,' invoking the prophetic/wisdom tradition.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'with oil' (שמן — anointing oil). Greek: κολλούριον ('eye-salve'). Entirely different substances.
Hebrew: 'my counsel' (noun, עצתי). Greek: 'I counsel' (verb, συμβουλεύω). Different construction.
Greek adds πεπυρωμένον ἐκ πυρός ('refined by fire') after gold — absent from Hebrew.
Greek adds ἵνα πλουτήσῃς ('so that you may become rich') — absent from Hebrew.
Greek adds καὶ μὴ φανερωθῇ ἡ αἰσχύνη τῆς γυμνότητός σου ('and the shame of your nakedness not be revealed') — absent from Hebrew. The Hebrew is dramatically more concise.
translation_notes: 'Anoint' for mashach — preserving the Messianic/priestly anointing verb.
'Counsel' for etsah — the specific word for divine/wise counsel in the prophetic tradition.
מַלְבּוּשִׁים (malbushim, H4403 — 'garments/clothing') — from root לבש (lavash — 'to clothe'). Different from בגדים (begadim) used in vv4-5; malbush emphasizes the garment as clothing to put on.
textual_notes: Isaiah 55:1 — 'Come, buy (שברו) wine and milk without money and without price.' The invitation to 'buy from me' echoes Isaiah's free-of-charge invitation. The gold here is spiritual, not commercial.

verses.translation: And I chastise{H3256} those whom I have loved{H157}. And now, do teshuvah{H8666}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מוֹסֵר (moser — 'chastise/discipline,' from root יסר yasar, H3256) — ONE Hebrew word. Greek has ἐλέγχω καὶ παιδεύω ('I rebuke AND discipline') — TWO words. The Hebrew collapses two Greek concepts into one word. Hebrew מוסר (musar — 'discipline/instruction') is THE central concept of Proverbs (Prov 1:2,7, 3:11, 12:1, 13:24, 15:5). A back-translator from Greek's two words would use two Hebrew words (e.g., מוכיח ומיסר), not collapse them into one.

DIRECT ECHO of Proverbs 3:12 — כִּי אֶת אֲשֶׁר יֶאֱהַב יְהוָה יוֹכִיחַ ('For whom YHWH loves he disciplines'). The Hebrew Revelation uses the same love-discipline pairing. Greek uses φιλῶ (phileō — 'friendship love'), NOT ἀγαπάω (agapaō). Hebrew uses אָהַבְתִּי (ahavti — from ahav, H157), the deep covenant love of the OT. A back-translator from Greek phileō might use חבב (chibev — 'to cherish') or ריע (rea — 'friend'), NOT the covenantal ahav.
Uses תְּשׁוּבָה (teshuvah) again — the same Hebrew repentance concept from v3. Greek has μετανόησον. See v3 notes.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: one verb מוסר ('chastise'). Greek: two verbs ἐλέγχω καὶ παιδεύω ('rebuke and discipline').
Hebrew: אהבתי (ahavti — 'I have loved,' PAST tense, covenantal love). Greek: φιλῶ (philō — 'I love,' PRESENT tense, friendship love). Different tense and different type of love.
Greek adds ζήλωσον ('be zealous') before 'repent' — absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Chastise' for moser — capturing the musar/discipline concept central to Proverbs.
'Teshuvah' left untranslated — see note on v3.
textual_notes: Proverbs 3:11-12 — 'My son, do not despise the discipline (מוסר) of YHWH, nor loathe his reproof; for whom YHWH loves (יאהב) he disciplines.' The Hebrew Revelation directly echoes this Proverbs passage.

verses.translation: See{H7200}! I stand{H5975} before{H6440} the opening{H6607} and knock{H1849} upon it. And if one hears{H8085} my voice{H6963} and opens{H6605} the opening{H6607}, to this one I will go{H1980}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: The פתח wordplay chain from v7-8 CONTINUES here: הַפֶּתַח (ha-petach — 'the opening') appears TWICE, and יִפְתַּח (yiftach — 'he opens') uses the same root. In v7: מַפְתֵּחַ (key) and פּוֹתֵחַ (opener) and לִפְתּוֹחַ (to open). In v8: פֶּתַח פָּתוּחַ (open opening). Now in v20: הפתח ... ויפתח הפתח. This extended five-verse פתח wordplay (vv7-8-20) is a deliberate structural feature ONLY visible in Hebrew. Greek uses three different roots: κλείς (key), θύρα (door), and ἀνοίγω (open) — no wordplay possible.

Uses דֹפֵק (dofek — 'knock,' from dafaq H1849). This EXACT form appears in Song of Songs 5:2 — קוֹל דּוֹדִי דוֹפֵק ('the voice of my beloved knocks'). The Hebrew Revelation echoes the Song of Songs' language of the beloved knocking at the door. A back-translator from Greek κρούω ('knock') could use דפק, but the Song of Songs echo (voice + knock at the opening) would be coincidental rather than deliberate.

Hebrew: לָזֶה אֵלֵךְ ('to this one I will go') — ONLY this. Greek adds: καὶ εἰσελεύσομαι πρὸς αὐτὸν καὶ δειπνήσω μετ' αὐτοῦ καὶ αὐτὸς μετ' ἐμοῦ ('and I will enter to him and dine with him and he with me'). The ENTIRE dining/fellowship clause is ABSENT from Hebrew. If the Hebrew were a back-translation from Greek, omitting such a beloved and vivid image of intimate table fellowship would be inexplicable.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: הפתח ('opening,' from root פתח). Greek: θύραν ('door'). Different nouns, breaking the Hebrew wordplay.
Greek adds the entire clause about dining together (δειπνήσω μετ' αὐτοῦ καὶ αὐτὸς μετ' ἐμοῦ) — absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: אלך ('I will go' — from halakh). Greek: εἰσελεύσομαι ('I will enter' — from eiserchomai). Hebrew implies walking toward; Greek implies entering into.
translation_notes: 'Opening' for petach — maintaining the consistent פתח translation throughout the chapter (vv7-8-20).
'Knock' for dofek — the Song of Songs verb for the beloved's knock.
לִפְנֵי (lifnei — 'before/in the face of') — more personal than merely 'at.' The speaker stands face-to-face with the opening.
textual_notes: Song of Songs 5:2 — 'I sleep but my heart is awake: the voice of my beloved knocks (דופק). Open (פתחי) to me, my sister, my darling, my dove.' The Hebrew Revelation combines 'voice' + 'knock' + 'open' (פתח), exactly as in Song of Songs.

verses.translation: Whoever overcomes{H5329}, to this one I will give{H5414} to sit{H3427} with me upon my throne{H3678}, just as I overcame{H5329} and sat{H3427} with my Father{H1} upon his throne{H3678}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כִּסֵּא (kise, H3678 — 'throne/seat') — the standard OT throne word (1 Kings 1:37,46; 2:12,19; Ps 45:6, 89:14, 93:2, 97:2). This is the throne of Solomon, of David, and of YHWH. Greek θρόνος is equivalent, but the Hebrew naturally draws from the OT throne vocabulary.

The parallel structure מְנַצֵּחַ/נִצַּחְתִּי (menatzeach/nitzachti — 'overcomes/I overcame') using the SAME root נצח (natsach, H5329) in both participial and perfect forms creates a Hebrew verbal echo: the overcomer's action mirrors the speaker's completed action. The root נצח in the OT means 'to oversee/direct/be victorious' (used in Psalm titles for the מנצח — director/choirmaster). The overcomer participates in the same נצח as the Mashiach.
translation_notes: 'Sit' for yoshev (H3427) — the verb of enthronement and settled authority (Ps 2:4 — 'He who sits in the heavens laughs'; Ps 110:1 — 'Sit at my right hand').
textual_notes: Psalm 110:1 — 'YHWH said to my lord: Sit (שב) at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool.' The invitation to sit on the throne echoes the Messianic enthronement psalm.

verses.translation: Whoever has ears{H241} hears{H8085} what the spirit{H7307} says{H559}.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew OMITS 'to the assemblies' (ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις) which Greek includes. The final refrain of the seven letters in Hebrew ends simply: 'what the spirit says' — without specifying the recipient. If the Hebrew were a back-translation from Greek, there would be no reason to drop 'to the assemblies' in this final instance. The omission may indicate that this concluding refrain universalizes the message — the spirit speaks not only to the assemblies but to all who hear.
greek_deviations: Greek adds ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις ('to the assemblies') — absent from Hebrew in this final refrain.
Same mood difference as v6 and v13: Hebrew indicative 'hears' vs. Greek imperative 'let him hear.'

chapter_notes.summary: Revelation 3 in Hebrew contains at least 20 clear one-way translation markers — cases where the Hebrew could not plausibly derive from the Greek text. The most striking are: (1) The five-verse פתח (patach) wordplay chain across vv7-8-20, where 'key' (mafteach), 'opener' (poteach), 'open opening' (petach patuach), and 'opening' (petach) all share one Hebrew root — a structural feature IMPOSSIBLE in Greek where κλείς, θύρα, and ἀνοίγω share no root. (2) The use of חַבְרוּתַת הַשָּׂטָן ('fellowship of the Adversary,' v9) instead of 'synagogue of Satan' — a distinctly rabbinic term no back-translator would choose. (3) The use of תְּשׁוּבָה ('returning,' vv3,19) instead of a calque of Greek metanoia ('mind-change'). (4) The use of שֶׁמֶן ('oil,' v18) for eye-anointing instead of Greek κολλούριον ('eye-salve') — with the verb מָשַׁח (mashach, root of Messiah). (5) The אָמֵן/נֶאֱמָן root-wordplay in v14 connecting the divine title 'Amen' to the attribute 'Faithful' through the shared root אמן. (6) The Song of Songs 5:2 echo in v20 — 'voice' + 'knock' (דופק) + 'open' (פתח). (7) The fixed OT word-pair עני ואביון ('poor and destitute,' v17) where Greek has five separate descriptors. (8) The use of ירק ('spit,' v16) — an act of Torah rejection — where Greek has 'vomit.' (9) The consistent use of עֵדָה (edah — Torah congregation) throughout for 'assembly.' The chapter also shows the Hebrew as systematically more concise than Greek, with Greek adding the 'pillar in the temple' clause (v12), the entire dining scene (v20), and multiple expansions (vv14,17,18). These patterns collectively point to Hebrew as the prior text from which the Greek was independently rendered.
